google-calendar-working-hours-location-o.title: Google Calendar working hours, working location, out of office or focus time: which one to set
google-calendar-working-hours-location-o.short: Working hours, location, OOO or focus time
google-calendar-working-hours-location-o.description: Pick the right Google Calendar availability signal: working hours, working location, out of office or focus time. See which ones decline meetings.
google-calendar-working-hours-location-o.lede: Google Workspace gives you four ways to tell colleagues about your time, and only two of them can turn down meetings for you. Choosing the wrong one either leaves your calendar looking open when you are not, or declines meetings you meant to attend. Arte Soft, the developer of Cloud Calendars, wrote this guide; every control below is Google’s own.
google-calendar-working-hours-location-o.commonBelief: Working location and out of office are two names for the same “I’m not at my desk” setting.

sections.heading: Four signals, four different questions
body: Working hours answer “when do I normally work?”. Working location answers “where am I working today?”. An out-of-office event answers “am I unavailable?”. Focus time answers “am I working but should not be interrupted?”. Treat them as separate answers rather than escalating levels of the same setting.

The distinction matters because of side effects. Google describes an out-of-office event as declining meetings while you are away, with optional decline settings and a message. Focus time has an “Automatically decline meetings” option. Working hours and working location are informational: Google documents them as showing people your availability and location, not as declining anything.

sections.heading: Set the weekly pattern first: working hours
body: On a computer, Google’s path is Settings, then under General, Working hours, then Enable working hours, choosing the days and times you work. To add more than one period in a day, such as a split shift or an overnight shift, use Add. Google requires each period’s start time to be before its end time and only supports working hours as a recurring weekly schedule.

Google says that if you travel, set a working location or change time zone, your working hours adjust to local time. For a one-off change such as an appointment, Google’s own advice is to edit your regular hours and then revert them; there is no separate one-day working-hours exception. On Android, Google directs you to calendar.google.com in a computer browser to set them. If the option is absent, Google says your administrator may not have turned it on.

sections.heading: Say where, not whether: working location
body: Working location needs working hours switched on first and an eligible edition; Google lists Business Standard, Business Plus, Enterprise Starter, Enterprise Standard, Enterprise Plus, Education Fundamentals, Education Standard, Education Plus and Nonprofits. Set a default per weekday under Settings, Working hours & location, choosing Home, Office or another location.

For one day, use the location chip at the top of the calendar and Edit working location. For part of a day, click an empty slot and choose Working location at the top of the new entry, then set the times. A working location is not the address of a meeting: it describes where you are, while each event keeps its own location field.

Google states that people with free/busy access to your calendar can see your availability and working location. Before choosing a precise address over “Home” or “Office”, consider who already has that level of access.

sections.heading: Decline on purpose: out of office and focus time
body: Create an out-of-office event with Create, then Out of office, and pick the dates. For a partial day, deselect All day. It can repeat, and Google marks the decline settings and message as optional changes. Google also says your status can be shown to people who email you, provided they have access to your calendar and the out-of-office event lasts the whole day or runs past your regular working hours.

Focus time is created from Day or Week view on a specific start and end time, then Focus time at the top of the event. Google says it declines new and existing meetings by default, and lets you limit that to only new meeting invitations. The first time you use it, Do not disturb for Chat is turned on; Google allows Chat muting only for blocks under 24 hours. Google lists Business Standard and Plus, Enterprise Standard and Plus, Education and Nonprofits editions for focus time.

“New and existing meetings” is the setting with consequences for other people: meetings you had already accepted inside the block can be declined. If you only want to protect empty time, choose new invitations only.

sections.heading: Worked example: one illustrative week
body: A fictional support lead works Monday to Thursday, 08:00–12:00 and 13:00–16:30, and takes Friday off. They set working hours with two periods on each of those days and leave Friday unticked. Their default location is Office; on Tuesday they add a part-day working location of Home until 12:00 and Office afterwards.

On Wednesday 09:00–11:00 they need uninterrupted time but have already accepted a 10:00 customer call. They create focus time and choose “Only new meeting invitations” so the accepted call survives. Friday gets an all-day out-of-office event with a short decline message naming a colleague to contact.

Check: open Wednesday and confirm the 10:00 call still shows as accepted; open Friday and confirm the out-of-office entry spans the whole day. If a meeting was declined that you meant to keep, open it, change your response and tell the organiser, because the decline was already sent.

sections.heading: Where Cloud Calendars fits
body: These four controls live in Google Calendar for Workspace accounts. Set and edit them there. This guide does not describe a Cloud Calendars control for creating them, and a calendar overview on your phone is not a substitute for checking how Google recorded your status.

cells: Used to show people your availability
Settings → Working hours; weekly pattern only, split periods via Add
Where you work today or part of a day
People with free/busy access or more
Requires working hours on; eligible editions only
Yes, with optional decline settings and message
Calendar viewers; Gmail senders who have calendar access
Create → Out of office; partial days by deselecting All day
Yes: new and existing by default, or new only
Day or Week view, timed block; eligible editions only

practical: Turn on working hours first; add a second period for split days.
Set a default working location per weekday, then override single days or part days with the location chip or a Working location entry.
Use out of office when you are unavailable, and write a decline message that names an alternative contact.
Use focus time when you are working but protecting time; choose “Only new meeting invitations” if accepted meetings in that block must stay.
After saving, reopen affected days and check that no meeting you need was declined; if one was, change your response and tell the organiser.

faq.q: Does setting my working location to Home decline in-person meetings?
faq.a: No. Google documents working location as information about where you work, visible to people with free/busy access or more. It does not decline invitations; use out of office or focus time when you need declines.

faq.q: Can I set different working hours just for next Tuesday?
faq.a: Google only supports working hours as a weekly recurring schedule and suggests editing your regular hours and reverting them afterwards. A part-day working location or an out-of-office block may describe a one-off change better.

faq.q: Why can’t I find working location or focus time?
faq.a: Both are limited to particular Google Workspace editions, and working location also requires working hours to be on. Google says an administrator may not have enabled the feature. A personal Google account will not show them.

faq.q: Will focus time decline a meeting I already accepted?
faq.a: By default Google says focus time declines new and existing meetings. Choose “Only new meeting invitations” before saving if you want existing acceptances to stand.

google-calendar-event-visibility-private.title: Google Calendar private events: what each person with access actually sees
google-calendar-event-visibility-private.description: See what Default, Public and Private event visibility show to each Google Calendar permission level, and why a Public event can expose a busy-only calendar.
google-calendar-event-visibility-private.lede: Marking an event Private feels like closing a door, but who is on the other side depends on the calendar’s sharing. Marking one Public can do the opposite of what people expect. This guide crosses Google’s three event visibility options with its calendar permission levels so you can predict the result before you save.
google-calendar-event-visibility-private.commonBelief: Private hides an event from everyone, and Public only matters on a public calendar.

sections.heading: Two settings decide what someone sees
body: Calendar sharing sets a person’s baseline: Google’s levels are “See only free/busy (hide details)”, “See all event details”, “Make changes (see private events as free/busy)”, “Make changes and see event details” and “Make changes and manage sharing”. Event visibility then adjusts that baseline for one event: Default visibility, Public or Private.
Default visibility follows the calendar’s sharing settings, so it changes nothing. The other two override the baseline in opposite directions, which is where surprises happen.

sections.heading: Public widens access for that one event
body: Google defines Public as: anyone who has access to view your calendar can see all the details of this event, even if your overall calendar is restricted to free/busy. A colleague who normally sees only grey busy blocks will see the title, place and description of that one event.

This is useful for, say, an office-hours slot you want everyone with access to read. It is a poor choice for anything you would not show to every person and group on your sharing list, including organisation-wide or public sharing if you have it.

sections.heading: Private narrows access, but not for everyone
body: Google says Private hides all details from everyone except you and people with “Make changes and see event details” or higher. So a co-manager with that level still reads your private events in full. Someone with “Make changes (see private events as free/busy)” does not.

What the others see depends on the event’s availability. Google states that a private event marked Busy appears as a busy block with no details, and a private event marked Free does not appear on your calendar at all for them.

Private is about people viewing your calendar. Google notes that when you invite someone to an event, they control how it shows on their own calendar. Guests of a private event still receive its details through the invitation.

sections.heading: Worked example: one appointment, four viewers
body: A fictional manager adds “Contract renewal — Northwind, Room 4” on Thursday at 14:00 and marks it Private and Busy. Their calendar is shared four ways: a team Google Group with free/busy only, a peer with See all event details, an assistant with Make changes (see private events as free/busy), and a deputy with Make changes and see event details.

The group, the peer and the assistant each see a busy block at 14:00 with no title. The deputy sees the full entry. If the manager had marked it Private and Free, the first three would see nothing at all at 14:00 and might book over it. If it had been marked Public, all four would see the title and room.

Recovery check: if a Public event was a mistake, set it back to Default visibility and save, then remember that anyone who already looked may have read it. Changing visibility affects what is shown from now on; it does not recall what was seen.

sections.heading: Change and verify one event
body: Open the event, choose edit, find the visibility control (shown as Default visibility until changed), pick Default visibility, Public or Private, and save. For tasks, Google says only tasks with a start and end time can have their visibility changed; tasks without times are always private.

To verify without exposing real data, ask a colleague who holds a known permission level to look at a harmless test event you mark Private and Busy, then Public. Do not share your account credentials to “see what they see”. On a work or school account, Google notes your administrator can limit sharing or turn off permission settings, so the levels you see may be fewer.

comparison.heading: What each viewer sees for one event (from Google’s definitions)

cells: Make changes (see private events as free/busy)
Make changes and see event details

practical: List who has each permission level on the calendar before relying on Private.
Mark sensitive events Private and Busy if others must still avoid booking over them.
Use Public only for events every person with any access may read.
Remember that guests receive event details through the invitation regardless of Private.
Test with a harmless event and a colleague who holds a known permission level.

faq.q: My assistant can edit my calendar. Can they read my private events?
faq.a: It depends on the exact level. Google’s “Make changes (see private events as free/busy)” shows private events as free/busy only; “Make changes and see event details” and “Make changes and manage sharing” show them in full.

faq.q: Why did a colleague with busy-only access see my event title?
faq.a: The event was probably marked Public. Google says Public reveals the event’s details to anyone who can view your calendar, even when the calendar is restricted to free/busy.

faq.q: Why can people book over my private appointment?
faq.a: If it is Private and marked Free, Google says it does not appear for people without detail access. Mark it Busy so it shows as a busy block.

google-appointment-schedule-which-calend.title: Google appointment schedule: which calendars and events block a booking slot
google-appointment-schedule-which-calend.short: Why a booking slot is open or hidden
google-appointment-schedule-which-calend.description: Diagnose why a Google appointment schedule shows or hides a slot: conflict calendars, Busy vs Free events, RSVPs, all-day events and date exceptions.
google-appointment-schedule-which-calend.lede: A booking page is only as trustworthy as the calendars it checks. When a client books over your dentist slot or cannot find Tuesday at all, the cause is usually a specific, checkable setting. This is a diagnostic for Google appointment schedules, written by Arte Soft, which develops Cloud Calendars and does not run Google’s booking pages.
google-appointment-schedule-which-calend.commonBelief: A booking page automatically avoids everything I can see in my calendar view.

sections.heading: What Google says blocks a slot
body: Google states that appointment times during events set to Busy do not appear on the booking page, and that no times appear on a day with an all-day event set to Busy. It also says that an event you have RSVPed Yes or Maybe to, or any busy event in a calendar reviewed for conflicts, does not appear as open.

The calendars reviewed are, in Google’s words, your primary calendar and any calendars you own, manage or are subscribed to — but only those you select. Open the schedule, choose Edit appointment schedule, then Calendars, and tick the calendars to check for conflicts. Google notes that checking secondary calendars requires an eligible Google Workspace or Google One plan, and that a schedule created on a shared calendar may not let you select other calendars.

sections.heading: Where Google’s pages disagree: tentative and Maybe
body: One Google page says Yes and Maybe responses block time. Another says unaccepted or tentative Google Calendar events do not block appointment availability. These may describe different states, but the wording overlaps. Do not rely on a Maybe response to protect a slot. If the time matters, put a Busy event on a checked calendar or use adjusted availability.

sections.heading: Date exceptions and booking rules
body: For holidays and unusual days, use adjusted availability rather than rewriting the weekly pattern. Google lets you choose specific dates where you are more or less available, and Unavailable all day for a date you cannot take bookings. Adjustments can also cover dates outside a recurring schedule with start and end dates.

Other settings hide slots for reasons unrelated to conflicts. Google applies a 4-hour minimum notice by default, and you can set a maximum number of bookings per day and buffer time between appointments. A slot that looks free on your calendar may still be hidden because of one of these rules.

sections.heading: Worked example: a tutor’s Tuesday
body: A fictional tutor offers 30-minute sessions 15:00–18:00 from their primary calendar. They also own a Family calendar and subscribe to a School term dates calendar. Only the primary calendar is ticked under Calendars.

On Tuesday a Family event “Pick-up” 16:00–16:30 is marked Busy, but the 16:00 slot still appears, because Family is not checked. A primary-calendar event “Lunch with Sam” at 15:00 marked Free also leaves 15:00 open. A team meeting at 17:00 accepted with Maybe may or may not block 17:00, given the conflicting Google wording. And at 13:00 the same day, nothing before 17:00 can be booked because of the default 4-hour notice.

Fixes in order: tick Family under Calendars (if the plan allows secondary calendars), change “Lunch with Sam” to Busy if it should block, add a Busy hold at 17:00 instead of trusting Maybe, and decide whether 4 hours’ notice suits you. Then reload the public booking page in a private browser window and confirm which slots appear.

sections.heading: Verify the fix from the visitor’s side
body: Your own calendar view is not the test. Open the booking page link as a visitor, check the specific day and time, and compare with a list of what you expect to see. Repeat after each change; changing several settings at once makes it hard to tell which one mattered.

If a client has already booked a slot that should have been blocked, the booking exists independently of your corrected settings. Contact them and use Google’s cancellation or rescheduling route for that appointment rather than deleting the event silently.

cells: Slot open over a busy personal event
Event’s calendar not selected for conflicts, or plan does not allow secondary calendars
Edit appointment schedule → Calendars; check plan eligibility
Slot open over an event in a checked calendar
An all-day Busy event, or Unavailable all day in adjusted availability
Make the all-day event Free if it should not block; review adjusted availability
Later slots missing on a busy day
Maximum bookings per day reached, or buffer time
Schedule was created on a shared calendar
Recreate the schedule on your own calendar if conflict checks are essential

practical: List the calendars that hold commitments you must protect.
Tick each of them under Edit appointment schedule → Calendars, checking plan eligibility for secondary calendars.
Mark events that should block as Busy, including all-day ones; do not rely on Maybe responses.
Use adjusted availability for holidays instead of editing the weekly pattern.
Reload the booking page as a visitor after each change and compare with your expected slots.

faq.q: Does my booking page check every calendar I can see?
faq.a: No. Google reviews the calendars you select for conflicts; your primary, owned, managed and subscribed calendars are eligible, and secondary calendars need an eligible plan.

faq.q: Why can a client book during my Free-marked lunch?
faq.a: Google blocks slots for events set to Busy. An event marked Free does not block a slot.

faq.q: How do I close the page for a bank holiday without changing every week?
faq.a: Use adjusted availability for that date and choose Unavailable all day.

google-calendar-change-event-owner-befor.title: Change the owner of a Google Calendar event before you hand over a meeting
google-calendar-change-event-owner-befor.short: Hand a meeting to a new owner
google-calendar-change-event-owner-befor.description: Transfer a Google Calendar event to a colleague, see the 60-day acceptance window and 200-guest limit, and check the Google Meet consequences before you leave.
google-calendar-change-event-owner-befor.lede: When you change roles, the meetings you organise do not follow your job title. Until someone else owns them, you remain the organiser, and a Meet link can depend on you staying in the organisation. Arte Soft, the developer of Cloud Calendars, wrote this checklist; the transfer itself happens in Google Calendar on a computer.
google-calendar-change-event-owner-befor.commonBelief: Sending a colleague “Change owner” hands the meeting over immediately.

sections.heading: What a transfer does and does not do
body: Google’s steps are: select an event you own, open Options, choose Change owner, enter the new owner and a message. The new owner receives an email with a link. Google states they have 60 days to accept and that you remain the owner until then.

For work or school accounts, the new owner must be in the same organisation. Google also says events with more than 200 guests cannot be transferred to another owner or calendar. Moving an event between your own calendars is a different action and does not change the organiser.

sections.heading: The Google Meet consequence
body: Google’s Meet documentation says that when an event is created on or transferred to someone else’s primary calendar, that person becomes the calendar event organiser, and the meeting’s features depend on the video-conferencing policies that apply to them. Its example: if the new organiser’s edition or admin settings do not allow recording, they will not be able to record the meeting.

If an event is instead put on a non-primary calendar, Google says the organiser does not change, so Meet features stay the same — and if you then leave the organisation before the meeting, the link stops working. Parking meetings on a team calendar is therefore not a safe substitute for a real owner transfer when you are leaving.

sections.heading: Worked example: a handover list
body: A fictional programme coordinator moving teams on 30 November organises three items: a weekly partner check-in, a one-off quarterly review with a Meet link that is usually recorded, and an all-hands briefing with 240 guests.

The check-in and review can be transferred to the incoming coordinator, who is in the same organisation. Before transferring the review, the coordinator asks whether the new owner’s account can record Meet calls; if not, recording will not be available after acceptance. The all-hands has more than 200 guests, so it cannot be transferred: the new coordinator creates a replacement event and the old one is cancelled with a note pointing to it.
The coordinator sends the transfers at least a week before leaving, then checks daily until each is accepted. On acceptance they open each event and confirm that it shows the new organiser.

sections.heading: Checks after acceptance
body: Open the event as the new owner and confirm the organiser, guest list, time zone and Meet link. Ask the new owner to start the Meet call briefly before the first real session if recording or other host features matter. For a recurring meeting, look at several future occurrences, not only the next one, before assuming the whole series moved.

If the transfer has not been accepted when you leave, you are still the owner. Do not let the 60-day window run out silently: chase the recipient or plan a replacement event with the attendees informed.

sections.heading: What this page does not cover
body: Transferring ownership of a whole secondary calendar is a different decision with its own consequences and is handled in a separate guide. Cloud Calendars can display Google events but does not perform Google’s ownership transfer; use Google Calendar for that step.

cells: Change owner, accepted, to colleague’s primary calendar
Low; check recording and host features
Change owner sent, not yet accepted
No (you remain owner for up to 60 days)
High; meeting still depends on you
Google says the Meet link stops working if you leave the organisation
Create a replacement owned by the successor

practical: List every event you organise that will outlive your role.
Confirm the successor is in the same organisation and ask whether their account supports the Meet features you rely on.
Send Change owner with a message well before your last day.
For events over 200 guests, have the successor create a replacement and cancel the original with a pointer.
Chase acceptances; you remain owner until each is accepted.
After acceptance, check the organiser, several recurring occurrences and the Meet link.

faq.q: Is the meeting transferred as soon as I click Change owner?
faq.a: No. Google says the new owner gets an email link, has 60 days to accept, and you stay owner until then.

faq.q: Can I transfer a meeting to someone at a client company?
faq.a: Not from a work or school account: Google requires the new owner to be in the same organisation.

faq.q: Will recording still work after the transfer?
faq.a: Only if the new organiser’s edition and admin settings allow it. Google says Meet features follow the policies of the calendar event organiser.

google-calendar-find-a-time-blank-is-not.title: Google Calendar Find a time: a blank column does not mean the guest is free
google-calendar-find-a-time-blank-is-not.description: Before booking into a gap in Google Calendar’s Find a time, check calendar sharing, private Free events and the 50-guest limit. A blank can mean no access.
google-calendar-find-a-time-blank-is-not.lede: Find a time lays guests’ calendars side by side so you can spot a common gap. The trap is that it can only draw what each guest has shared with you. This guide gives a short diagnostic for deciding whether a gap is real before you send the invitation.
google-calendar-find-a-time-blank-is-not.commonBelief: If Find a time shows nothing for a guest at 15:00, they are free at 15:00.

sections.heading: How Find a time works, per Google
body: On a computer, choose Create, then Event, add guests, then Find a time. Google says you can compare availability for up to 50 guests; if you add more, only 50 schedules are shown. You can filter to show no guests, required guests or all guests, toggle rooms, and use the Day view to compare calendars in separate columns rather than overlapping.

The key condition is Google’s own: these guests must have shared their calendars with you. If a person does not share their calendar with you, Google says you can send them a request to share it. Rooms are added with Add rooms or Add room booking.

sections.heading: Four reasons a gap may not be free
body: No access. A guest who has not shared a calendar with you has nothing to draw. Their column can look empty without telling you anything about their day.

Private and Free. Google says a private event marked Free does not appear on the calendar for people without detail-level access. If a guest marks personal appointments that way, you cannot see them, by design.
Not on a shared calendar. You see only what the guest shared. Commitments they keep on other calendars, or in another account, are outside the view.
Over 50 guests. Beyond 50, Google shows only 50 schedules. A large invitation’s comparison is necessarily partial; use the Required guests filter to focus on people whose attendance decides the time.

sections.heading: Worked example: picking a slot for five people
body: A fictional organiser needs one hour on Thursday with four colleagues and an external consultant. Find a time shows three colleagues busy 10:00–12:00 and free 14:00–15:00. The fourth colleague’s column is empty all day. The consultant, outside the organisation, also shows nothing.

The organiser does not treat 14:00 as agreed. They check whether the fourth colleague shares their calendar; they do not, so the organiser requests access or simply asks. The consultant’s availability is unknown, so the organiser sends two candidate times by message before inviting. Once both reply, the organiser books 14:00 and adds a room through Add room booking.
Result check: after sending, open the event and watch the responses. A Yes from each required guest, not the empty column, confirms the slot.

sections.heading: Make your own calendar readable to schedulers
body: If colleagues keep booking over you, the fix is on your side. Share your calendar with at least free/busy access with the people who schedule you, and mark private appointments Busy rather than Free so they show as blocks without details. Workspace users can also set working hours and a working location, which Google says people with free/busy access can see.
Check your own sharing in your calendar’s settings and, if you are on a work or school account, remember that an administrator may limit the sharing options available.

cells: Has this guest shared a calendar with you?
Gaps are at least partly meaningful
Request access or ask the guest directly
Could they keep private events marked Free?
Those events are invisible to you
Ask, or rely on their response to the invitation
More than 50 guests on the event?
Usually no shared calendar in your view
Agree candidate times by message first

practical: Add guests, then open Find a time and switch to Required guests.
For each empty column, check whether that person shares a calendar with you.
Request access or ask directly when a column is blank.
Treat the invitation responses, not the gap, as confirmation.
Share at least free/busy and mark private appointments Busy so others can schedule around you.

faq.q: Why does one colleague always look free in Find a time?
faq.a: Most likely they have not shared their calendar with you. Google’s Find a time only compares guests who have shared their calendars.

faq.q: Can Find a time see private appointments?
faq.a: It shows what the sharing allows. A private event marked Busy appears as a busy block; Google says one marked Free does not appear for people without detail access.

faq.q: Is there a guest limit?
faq.a: Google compares availability for up to 50 guests; beyond that only 50 schedules are shown.

outlook-calendar-delegate-or-editor-perm.title: Outlook calendar: give an assistant Can edit or Delegate access?
outlook-calendar-delegate-or-editor-perm.description: Choose Can edit or Delegate for an Outlook calendar, decide on private items and meeting-request routing, and avoid unsupported delegate setups.
outlook-calendar-delegate-or-editor-perm.lede: In Outlook, someone who can change your calendar is not necessarily someone who handles your meetings. Microsoft separates the two, and the extra delegate options decide whether your invitations go to you, to them, or to both. Arte Soft, the developer of Cloud Calendars, wrote this guide to the owner’s side of that decision.
outlook-calendar-delegate-or-editor-perm.commonBelief: Edit access and delegate access are the same thing with different names.

sections.heading: The difference in one sentence each
body: Microsoft says Can edit lets the person view and make changes to your calendar. Delegate lets them edit your calendar items and, in addition, schedule and respond to meetings on your behalf.

So the question is not how much you trust the person but which job they do. A colleague maintaining a team rota needs Can edit. An assistant who accepts, declines and sends invitations for you needs Delegate. Microsoft states that you cannot give editor or delegate access to people outside your organisation, and that delegate access requires a work or school account in Microsoft 365 or Exchange Online.

sections.heading: Delegate options that change your inbox
body: When you choose Delegate, Microsoft lets you decide where meeting requests and responses go: to your delegates only, to your delegates with a copy to you, or to both you and your delegates. Pick deliberately. If requests go only to the delegate, you will not see new invitations arrive yourself.

Microsoft also offers “Let delegate view private events”. Without it, most people you share with see only the time of items marked Private, not the subject, location or other details. A separate option lets a delegate manage categories, so colour-coding is not automatically part of delegate access.

sections.heading: Classic delegate levels in Exchange
body: Microsoft’s delegate overview describes three per-folder levels. Reviewer can read items. Author can read and create items and change or delete items they created. Editor can do everything an Author can and also change and delete items you created.
Author is a sensible middle ground for someone who adds holds to your calendar but should not touch meetings you set up. Editor is needed when they must rework your existing entries.

sections.heading: Setups Microsoft advises against
body: Microsoft’s organisational best practice recommends granting Editor to only one delegate and avoiding many delegates with Reviewer or Contributor permissions; it says its testing used a maximum of four delegates. It also states that setting a security group as a delegate is not supported — add individual people instead.
Two editing delegates processing the same requests can leave meetings in conflicting states. If you need cover during absences, name one primary delegate and agree when the backup acts.

sections.heading: Worked example: a director and two helpers
body: A fictional director has an executive assistant who runs their diary and a project coordinator who adds review sessions. The assistant gets Delegate, with requests sent to the delegate with a copy to the director, and “Let delegate view private events” ticked because they need to work around private appointments. The coordinator gets Can edit only.

The director keeps a few entries Private. The coordinator sees those as time only; the assistant sees their details. Nobody else is a delegate, and the director does not add the whole admin team as a security-group delegate.

Check: the assistant accepts the sharing invitation, which Microsoft says adds the director’s calendar to their list. The director sends a test invitation from a colleague and confirms it reaches both inboxes as chosen.

sections.heading: Cloud Calendars and delegated calendars
body: Cloud Calendars’ Microsoft connection is part of its Premium plan, but general Microsoft capabilities do not guarantee that every delegated or shared-mailbox calendar appears in a third-party app. Grant and test delegation in Outlook itself.

faq.q: Can my delegate see my private appointments?
faq.a: Only if you tick “Let delegate view private events”. Otherwise Microsoft says most people see just the time of private items.

faq.q: Can I make an external virtual assistant my delegate?
faq.a: No. Microsoft states you cannot give editor or delegate access to people outside your organisation.

faq.q: How many delegates should I have?
faq.a: Microsoft recommends only one delegate with Editor permissions and avoiding large numbers of delegates; its testing used up to four.

outlook-schedule-meeting-on-behalf-of-so.title: Schedule a meeting on someone else’s Outlook calendar: save, send and check
outlook-schedule-meeting-on-behalf-of-so.description: As an Outlook delegate, save a meeting to the owner’s calendar, know what attendees see, and avoid the one choice Microsoft says cannot be changed later.
outlook-schedule-meeting-on-behalf-of-so.lede: When you organise meetings for a manager, the meeting has to land on their calendar, not yours. In Outlook on the web that hinges on one field, and Microsoft says it cannot be changed once the invitation is sent. This guide walks through the delegate’s side of the job.
outlook-schedule-meeting-on-behalf-of-so.commonBelief: If I can see my manager’s calendar, any meeting I create will be theirs.

sections.heading: Before you start: permission and the calendar list
body: Microsoft says you can only edit someone else’s calendar after they give you permission by sharing it. Accept their sharing invitation to add their calendar to your list. When you create an event, Outlook on the web only offers calendars that are in your list and for which you hold editor or delegate permission.

If the owner’s calendar is missing from the list, the fix is on the permission side, not in your event form. Ask them to check what they granted; the owner’s decision between Can edit and Delegate is covered in a separate guide.

sections.heading: Create the meeting on the right calendar
body: Choose New event, then set the Save to calendar field to the owner’s calendar before adding attendees or sending. Microsoft states that once a meeting invitation has been sent, you cannot change the calendar on which it was scheduled.

That makes the practical recovery for a mis-filed meeting blunt: cancel it from the calendar where it was saved, then create it again on the correct calendar and tell the attendees why they received a cancellation and a new invitation.

sections.heading: What attendees see and where replies go
body: Microsoft says the invitation will show that it is from you on the calendar owner’s behalf. If you need messages to appear as sent directly by the owner, that is Send As permission, which Microsoft says only your organisation’s administrator can set.

If you are a delegate, Microsoft says meeting requests and updates are sent to you and appear in your inbox like any other request. Microsoft’s best practice is to process each one properly by accepting or declining it, and to use Remove from Calendar for cancellations, rather than deleting messages.

sections.heading: Worked example: a board pre-read session
body: A fictional assistant schedules a 45-minute pre-read for their director with three board members. In Outlook on the web they choose New event, set Save to calendar to the director’s calendar, add the attendees and a Teams link, and send.

The board members see an invitation from the assistant on behalf of the director. Their acceptances arrive in the assistant’s inbox, and the assistant opens each response rather than deleting it unread.

Mistake scenario: had the assistant left Save to calendar on their own calendar, the director would not be the organiser. The correction is to cancel that meeting and recreate it on the director’s calendar, with a short note to the board members.

sections.heading: Verify before the day
body: Open the owner’s calendar and confirm the meeting appears there with the right time zone and attendees. Check that responses are arriving where you expect. If the owner also processes the same requests, agree who acts on them to avoid conflicting replies.
Cloud Calendars, made by Arte Soft, can show Microsoft calendars on its Premium plan, but it does not provide Outlook’s Save to calendar or Send As controls. Schedule delegated meetings in Outlook.

faq.q: I sent the meeting from my own calendar by mistake. Can I move it?
faq.a: Microsoft says you cannot change the calendar once the invitation has been sent. Cancel it and recreate it on the owner’s calendar.

faq.q: Why does the invitation say “on behalf of”?
faq.a: That is how Microsoft shows a meeting sent by a delegate. Sending as the owner without that label needs Send As, which only an administrator can grant.

faq.q: Why can’t I select my manager’s calendar in Save to calendar?
faq.a: Microsoft only lists calendars that are in your calendar list and for which you have editor or delegate permission.

outlook-calendar-sharing-levels-busy-tit.title: Outlook calendar sharing levels: busy only, titles and locations, or all details
outlook-calendar-sharing-levels-busy-tit.description: Compare Outlook’s calendar sharing levels with one example entry, see what private items show, and check the My organization default after removing access.
outlook-calendar-sharing-levels-busy-tit.lede: Outlook offers several sharing levels, and the difference between the first three is exactly the information a colleague learns about each appointment. Removing someone does not always take them to zero, because of an organisation-wide default. Arte Soft, the developer of Cloud Calendars, wrote this guide to Microsoft 365’s own sharing controls.
outlook-calendar-sharing-levels-busy-tit.commonBelief: Removing a colleague from my sharing list means they can no longer see anything on my calendar.

sections.heading: The levels, in Microsoft’s words
body: Microsoft lists: Can view when I’m busy (availability without details such as location), Can view titles and locations (availability plus titles and locations), Can view all details, Can edit, and Delegate. Can edit and Delegate are only available when sharing with people in your organisation.

Microsoft also says calendar items marked Private are protected: most people you share with see only the time of a private item, not its title or location, while delegates can be allowed to see details.

sections.heading: Worked example: one entry, three viewers
body: A fictional account manager has “Pricing review — Contoso — Room 3B, 14:00–15:00” on Thursday, not marked Private. A colleague with Can view when I’m busy sees that 14:00–15:00 is busy. A colleague with Can view titles and locations sees “Pricing review — Contoso” and “Room 3B” but not the notes or attachments. A colleague with Can view all details sees everything in the entry.
If the manager marks the entry Private, all three see only that 14:00–15:00 is taken. Choose the lowest level that lets each person do their job: scheduling around you needs only the first.

sections.heading: The My organization default
body: Outlook may list a “My organization” entry in sharing. Microsoft describes it as the default level colleagues get, for example when they use the Scheduling Assistant. When you remove a named person, Microsoft says that if My organization is set to anything other than None, that person’s view updates to the default level rather than disappearing.
So a colleague you remove from Can view all details may still see titles and locations if that is your organisation default. Check the My organization row after every removal.

sections.heading: Change, remove and confirm
body: In Outlook on the web, right-click the calendar name, choose Sharing and permissions, then select a new level or remove the person. Microsoft notes that calendar sharing may be unavailable for your account or limited to your organisation, depending on organisation settings.

Microsoft recommends the simplified levels over custom permissions. Intermediate permissions set with PowerShell show as Custom, and Microsoft states custom levels are not supported in the newer sharing model. If you see Custom, ask your administrator before assuming what it allows.

sections.heading: How recipients receive your calendar
body: In Microsoft’s newer model, a copy of your shared calendar is created in the recipient’s mailbox and changes sync to it promptly in supported apps, which Microsoft lists as Outlook for Windows, Mac, web, iOS and Android, plus REST and Exchange ActiveSync apps; Exchange Web Services is excluded. After an upgrade, Microsoft says the copy includes events from one year before the upgrade date and all future events.

Microsoft also warns that some Exchange ActiveSync apps let a read-only recipient try to create or respond to a meeting on your calendar; the change saves locally and is then rejected by the server. A recipient who “edited” your calendar on a phone may simply be seeing a rejected local change.

Grant the lowest level that does that job.

faq.q: Can “Can view when I’m busy” reveal where I am?
faq.a: Microsoft describes it as showing availability without details such as location. Titles and locations require the next level.

faq.q: I removed someone but they still see my appointment titles. Why?
faq.a: Microsoft says removed people fall back to the My organization default if it is set above None. Lower or remove that default.

faq.q: A colleague with view access says they moved my meeting on their phone.
faq.a: Microsoft notes that some ActiveSync apps let read-only recipients make local changes that the server then rejects. Check your calendar in Outlook.

outlook-share-calendar-outside-organizat.title: Share a Microsoft 365 calendar with someone outside your organisation
outlook-share-calendar-outside-organizat.description: Find out whether your admin, your sharing choice or the partner’s calendar service limits external Outlook calendar sharing, and what the partner receives.
outlook-share-calendar-outside-organizat.lede: Sharing a work calendar with a contractor or client involves three parties: your tenant’s administrator, you, and whatever calendar service the recipient uses. Each can limit the result. Arte Soft, the developer of Cloud Calendars, wrote this guide to help you find which one is limiting yours.
outlook-share-calendar-outside-organizat.commonBelief: If I can share my calendar with a colleague, I can share it the same way with anyone.

sections.heading: Layer one: what the administrator allows
body: Microsoft’s admin documentation places external calendar sharing under Microsoft 365 admin center, Settings, Org Settings, Services, Calendar. An administrator can let users share with people outside the organisation who have Office 365 or Exchange, and, only after that, allow anyone to access calendars with an email invitation.

For those anonymous recipients, the administrator chooses the maximum detail: free/busy with time only; free/busy with time, subject and location; or all calendar appointment information. Sharing with an on-premises Exchange organisation needs a federation relationship configured by the Exchange administrator.

sections.heading: Layer two: what you choose
body: Once the administrator enables it, Microsoft says users decide whether to share, how much and when to stop. In Outlook on the web you choose a level for the external address. Can edit and Delegate are only available for people in your organisation, and Microsoft separately states you cannot give editor or delegate access to people outside it.

Microsoft also notes that sharing may be unavailable for your account or limited to your organisation depending on organisation settings. A missing option is usually layer one, not a fault in your mailbox.

sections.heading: Layer three: what the recipient’s service does
body: Microsoft says that when you share with someone outside the organisation, an Internet Calendar Subscription (ICS) URL is generated, which they can add to any calendar service. Microsoft gives typical refresh behaviour of approximately every three hours, and potentially every 24–48 hours depending on the recipient’s service.

That means an external partner can be a day behind your changes through no fault of yours. For time-sensitive changes, tell them directly. Publishing a calendar as HTML or ICS from calendar settings is a separate, read-only route, and should not be used to work around a blocked share.

sections.heading: Worked example: a freelance designer
body: A fictional marketing lead wants a freelance designer with a personal email address to see when the team’s review slots are free. The lead tries to choose Can edit; it is not offered, because the designer is external. They choose Can view when I’m busy instead.

If the share option for the designer’s address is missing entirely, the lead asks IT whether external sharing and email-invitation access are enabled. If the designer reports that a review moved yesterday still shows the old time, the lead checks their own calendar, then explains that the designer’s calendar app refreshes the subscription on its own schedule and confirms the new time by message.
Result check: the designer sees busy blocks without titles, as intended; nothing editable has been granted.

faq.q: Can a client edit my Outlook calendar?
faq.a: No. Microsoft states that editor and delegate access cannot be given to people outside your organisation.

faq.q: Why does my contractor see changes so late?
faq.a: External recipients get an ICS subscription URL. Microsoft says it syncs about every three hours, or every 24–48 hours depending on their calendar service.

faq.q: The share option for external people is missing. Is my account broken?
faq.a: More likely your administrator has not enabled external calendar sharing. Microsoft notes sharing may be limited to your organisation by organisation settings.

outlook-show-as-free-busy-tentative-work.title: Outlook Show As: free, tentative, busy, working elsewhere or out of office
outlook-show-as-free-busy-tentative-work.description: Choose the right Outlook Show As status for each appointment and decide when automatic replies should block your calendar or decline meetings.
outlook-show-as-free-busy-tentative-work.lede: Every Outlook appointment carries a status that colleagues see when they try to book you. Accepting a meeting or adding an item usually marks the time Busy, which is not always what you mean. Arte Soft, the developer of Cloud Calendars, explains how to choose each status and when automatic replies should do the work instead.
outlook-show-as-free-busy-tentative-work.commonBelief: Out of office and Working elsewhere both just mean “not at my desk”.

sections.heading: The five statuses
body: Microsoft says appointments can be marked free, busy, tentative, out of the office or working elsewhere. Its developer reference defines them plainly: Free means available; Tentative means a tentative appointment is scheduled; Busy means busy; Out of office means out of the office; Working elsewhere means working in a location away from the office.

Microsoft states this choice affects the free/busy time others see when they try to schedule a meeting with you. It also says that, by default, when you add an item or accept an invitation in classic Outlook, the item is marked Busy.

sections.heading: Change the status of one item
body: In classic Outlook or new Outlook for Windows, right-click the item on your calendar, choose Show As, then the status. Do this for entries that should not block bookings, such as a reminder to submit expenses, which would otherwise default to Busy.

In the Scheduling Assistant, Microsoft says busy time shows in dark blue, tentative appointments as a light blue hashed block, and time outside attendees’ working hours in light grey. That is how a colleague will read your choice.

sections.heading: For whole periods away: automatic replies
body: For Outlook.com and Outlook on the web, Microsoft’s automatic replies settings include three calendar options alongside the reply message: “Block my calendar for this period”, “Automatically decline new invitations for events that occur during this period”, and “Decline and cancel my meetings during this period”. You can limit replies to a time period, and choose whether replies go outside your organisation.
The third option affects other people’s calendars, not just yours. Read the confirmation and consider telling attendees of meetings you organise before using it.

sections.heading: Worked example: one illustrative week
body: A fictional consultant marks Monday’s client workshop Busy. Tuesday they work from a partner’s site, so they add an all-day item marked Working elsewhere: colleagues can still contact them but should not book an in-office room. Wednesday’s “Maybe join the vendor demo” is Tentative. A Thursday lunchtime reminder to call the bank is Free so it does not block bookings.

Friday and the following Monday are leave. Rather than one Out of office item, the consultant turns on automatic replies for that period with “Block my calendar for this period” and “Automatically decline new invitations”. They do not tick “Decline and cancel my meetings” because a recurring team meeting they organise should still go ahead without them.
Check: open the Scheduling Assistant for a test meeting with yourself and a colleague and confirm the colours match your intent.

Use Working elsewhere for days you work away from your usual office.
Use Tentative for meetings you may attend.
For leave, use automatic replies with “Block my calendar” and “Automatically decline new invitations”.
Only use “Decline and cancel my meetings” after considering the attendees of meetings you organise.
Check the result in the Scheduling Assistant.

faq.q: Why does everything I accept show as Busy?
faq.a: Microsoft says that, by default in classic Outlook, items you add or invitations you accept are marked Busy. Change individual items with Show As.

faq.q: What is the difference between Working elsewhere and Out of office?
faq.a: Microsoft defines Working elsewhere as working away from the office and Out of office as out of the office. Use the first when you are still working.

faq.q: Will automatic replies cancel my meetings?
faq.a: Only if you choose “Decline and cancel my meetings during this period”. Blocking your calendar and declining new invitations are separate options.

outlook-forward-meeting-and-allow-forwar.title: Forwarding Outlook meetings: what attendees can do and how to stop it
outlook-forward-meeting-and-allow-forwar.description: What happens when an attendee forwards your Outlook meeting, how Allow forwarding works, and what attendees can still copy or reply after it is off.
outlook-forward-meeting-and-allow-forwar.lede: An attendee who forwards your meeting effectively adds a guest. Outlook tells the organiser in some cases and lets you switch forwarding off in others, but neither is a confidentiality guarantee. Arte Soft, the developer of Cloud Calendars, explains the controls and their limits.
outlook-forward-meeting-and-allow-forwar.commonBelief: Turning off Allow forwarding makes a meeting invitation impossible to pass on.

sections.heading: What forwarding does
body: Microsoft describes forwarding as the way to invite someone to a meeting you did not organise. The recipient’s request appears to come from the meeting organiser, and the organiser receives a notification that you forwarded it. Microsoft specifies that classic Outlook sends this meeting forward notification when the recipient was not originally invited.

For a recurring meeting, Microsoft lets you forward just this one occurrence or the entire series. If you are the organiser, Microsoft’s advice is not to forward your own meeting but to add the person as an attendee and send an update.

sections.heading: Turning forwarding off
body: As organiser, open Response Options while creating or editing the meeting and clear Allow forwarding. Microsoft says forwarding is allowed by default. Attendees then do not get the forward option.

Microsoft lists support for Microsoft 365 users of Outlook for Windows (version 1808 or later on Current Channel, 1902 or later on Semi-Annual Enterprise Channel), Outlook for Mac 16.20 or later, and Outlook on the web for Microsoft 365 and Exchange 2019. It says iOS and Android are not yet supported for this setting.

sections.heading: What still gets through
body: Microsoft is explicit that even with forwarding prevented, attendees can still reply or reply all to the invitation with an email message, and copy the meeting message or event. When an attendee uses an older client against an older Exchange version or a third-party service, the forward is handled by servers that do not support the feature, so it cannot be prevented.

Treat Allow forwarding as a guard against casual additions, not as access control. Keep sensitive material out of the invitation body and share documents with named people through their own permissions.

sections.heading: Worked example: a recruitment panel
body: A fictional hiring manager organises a 60-minute panel with three interviewers and does not want the slot passed around. They create the meeting in Outlook on the web, open Response options and clear Allow forwarding, and keep the candidate’s CV out of the invitation, sharing it with the three interviewers separately.

A fourth colleague later needs to join. One interviewer asks the manager instead of forwarding, and the manager adds the colleague as an attendee and sends an update. That keeps the attendee list in the organiser’s hands and avoids relying on forward notifications.
Check: open the meeting and confirm the attendee list matches the people you invited; compare with any forward notifications you received.

sections.heading: Two special cases
body: Delegates: Microsoft’s best practice notes that Outlook delegates do not receive meeting forward notifications. If an assistant manages your meetings, check the attendee list rather than expecting a notice.

Shared calendars: Microsoft documented a known issue in which Allow forwarding was missing from Response Options for a meeting on a shared calendar in Outlook for Microsoft 365 versions earlier than Version 2008 Build 13127.20296, fixed in that build; the workaround was to ensure Download Shared folder is checked for the shared mailbox.

If you only want to tell someone about a meeting without inviting them, Microsoft describes dragging the meeting to the Mail icon in classic Outlook to send its details by email; that email does not add the recipient to the meeting.

faq.q: Will I know if someone forwards my meeting?
faq.a: Microsoft says the organiser receives a meeting forward notification, which classic Outlook sends when the recipient was not originally invited. Delegates do not receive these notifications.

faq.q: Does turning off Allow forwarding stop all sharing of the invite?
faq.a: No. Microsoft says attendees can still reply with an email or copy the meeting, and forwards through older or third-party systems cannot be prevented.

faq.q: Can I prevent forwarding from the Outlook mobile app?
faq.a: Microsoft lists iOS and Android as not yet supported for this setting. Use Outlook on the web or the desktop app.

outlook-group-calendar-versus-shared-cal.title: Microsoft 365 group calendar or a shared calendar: who can cancel, who gets invited
outlook-group-calendar-versus-shared-cal.description: Choose a Microsoft 365 group calendar or a shared personal calendar for a team: who can edit or cancel events, and who actually gets invited.
outlook-group-calendar-versus-shared-cal.lede: A team schedule in Outlook can live on a Microsoft 365 group calendar or on one person’s calendar shared with the team. They behave differently in two ways that matter in practice: who can cancel an event, and whether members are invited at all. Arte Soft, the developer of Cloud Calendars, compares them.
outlook-group-calendar-versus-shared-cal.commonBelief: Putting an event on the group calendar invites everyone in the group.

sections.heading: Group calendar: shared ownership
body: Microsoft says each Microsoft 365 group has a shared calendar where every member can schedule, edit and see upcoming events. It also says that when an event is created on the group calendar, anyone in the group can cancel it — unlike an event on your own calendar, where you are in charge of editing or cancelling.
That suits a rota or shared deadlines list maintained by everyone. It does not suit a client meeting whose time only the organiser should control.

sections.heading: Invitations are not automatic
body: Microsoft states that by default, meeting invitations are not sent to every member’s inbox in the group. To invite them, add the group to the attendees list; new Outlook also offers an Invite members button. Microsoft says you, as creator, are automatically added as an attendee and the event appears on your personal calendar.
So an event can sit on the group calendar without appearing on members’ personal calendars or prompting a reply. If attendance matters, invite the group explicitly.

sections.heading: Shared personal calendar: one owner
body: The alternative is a calendar you own and share with the team at a chosen level: Can view when I’m busy, Can view titles and locations, Can view all details, Can edit or Delegate (the last two only inside your organisation). You decide who can change it, and can remove access later.
Do not try to give a whole team delegate rights through a security group: Microsoft’s best practice says setting a security group as a delegate is not supported.

sections.heading: Worked example: an events team
body: A fictional events team of six has two needs. First, a shared list of venue deadlines and staff on-site days, which any member updates. Second, client walkthroughs that the team lead schedules and that should not be moved by others.

Deadlines and on-site days go on the group calendar; members are not invited to each item, which avoids six inbox requests for every deadline. Client walkthroughs go on the lead’s own calendar with the client and relevant staff invited, and the lead shares that calendar with the team at Can view titles and locations.
Check: a member opens the group calendar and confirms they can edit a deadline; another member confirms they can see the walkthrough title but cannot move it.

cells: Who can edit or cancel events?
Only people you grant Can edit or Delegate
Not by default; add the group as attendee or use Invite members

practical: Put shared, low-stakes items on the group calendar.
Keep meetings whose time must not change on an owned calendar.
When creating a group-calendar event that needs attendance, add the group as an attendee.
Share your owned calendar at the lowest useful level instead of making everyone a delegate.
Test that a member can or cannot change an event as intended.

faq.q: Why didn’t members get an invitation for a group calendar event?
faq.a: Microsoft says invitations are not sent to every member by default. Add the group to the attendees list.

faq.q: A colleague cancelled an event I put on the group calendar. Is that allowed?
faq.a: Yes. Microsoft states anyone in the group can cancel an event created on the group calendar.

faq.q: Can I make a security group my delegate instead?
faq.a: Microsoft says setting a security group as a delegate is not supported; add individual people.
